solutions.check: grid rebuilt from the blog's light list (unique); every answer written into it with each crossing agreeing

clue.text: Disturbed grave, silent and deathless

indicators.note: a disturbed grave has been dug over and churned up, so its letters are rearranged along with the next word

explanation.surface: An undead figure rises from a desecrated, silent grave.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Disturbed' rearranges GRAVE and SILENT together; 'and' is only a link to the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: Something deathless never dies, so it lasts for ever, a straight synonym.

clue.text: Wild nettle's head in bloom

indicators.note: the nettle's head is set inside the word for the bloom

parts.note: a violet is a small purple flower, a bloom

indicators.note: the head of a word is its first letter, here taken from nettle

explanation.surface: A gardener complains that the top of a nettle has run riot among the flowers.
explanation.definitionFit: Wild and violent are synonyms for unrestrained, savage behaviour or weather.

clue.text: 'Express' in support for confinement

indicators.note: the express is placed inside the word for support

parts.note: a rest is something that supports, like an armrest
an express is a fast train

explanation.surface: A newspaper title seems to be propping up the case for locking someone up.
explanation.walkthrough: The quotation marks make 'Express' look like the British newspaper; here it is a fast train.
explanation.definitionFit: Restraint is the act of holding someone back or confining them.

clue.text: Jelly fish could be its source

definitions.text: Jelly fish could be its source

parts.words: Jelly fish could be its source
parts.note: read as a savoury jelly whose setting stock might come from fish, not as the sea creature

explanation.surface: A marine creature might be where a jelly comes from.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface runs 'Jelly fish' together as the sea creature; split it, and the clue describes a savoury jelly that can be set with fish stock.
explanation.definitionFit: Aspic is a clear savoury jelly made from meat or fish stock.

clue.text: Thrash tar's extremities with cat

indicators.note: the extremities of a word are its first and last letters, here of tar

parts.note: the ounce is the snow leopard, a big cat

explanation.surface: A sailor's limbs are lashed with a cat-o'-nine-tails.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Tar' is a sailor and 'cat' the whip in the surface; here tar just gives its outer letters and the cat is the snow leopard.
explanation.definitionFit: To trounce is to beat or defeat heavily, just as to thrash is.

clue.text: New, a perfume just coming out

parts.note: a scent is a perfume

explanation.surface: A new fragrance is just being launched.
explanation.definitionFit: Nascent describes something just coming into being, emerging.

clue.text: Opinion about left's behaviour

indicators.note: the opinion goes around the word for left

parts.note: a comment is an opinion expressed
port is the left side of a ship

explanation.surface: Someone passes judgement on a departed person's conduct.
explanation.definitionFit: Comportment is a formal word for the way someone behaves or bears themselves.

clue.text: FBI agent, alternatively American detective's hat?

parts.note: a fed is US slang for a federal agent
or introduces an alternative

explanation.surface: Is the federal agent or the American private eye the one in the trilby-style hat?
explanation.definitionFit: A fedora is the soft felt brimmed hat worn by film-noir private eyes, an example.

clue.text: Oppressive old emperor pursuing unscrupulous ends

indicators.note: the ends of unscrupulous follow behind the old emperor

parts.note: Nero was a notorious Roman emperor

indicators.note: the ends of a word are its first and last letters, here of unscrupulous

explanation.surface: A tyrannical ancient ruler chases dishonest goals.
explanation.definitionFit: Onerous means burdensome or heavy to bear, close to oppressive.

clue.text: Novelist's page put out about opening of 'Remembrance…'

indicators.note: page and put-out wrap around the opening of Remembrance

parts.note: to oust is to put out or expel

indicators.note: the opening of a word is its first letter, here of Remembrance

explanation.surface: A novelist's page is discarded around the start of his great work.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Remembrance…' nods to Remembrance of Things Past, the old English title of this novelist's masterpiece; the possessive in the definition is the 's link ('is').
explanation.definitionFit: Marcel Proust was the French author of In Search of Lost Time.

clue.text: Colour's run with material ruined

indicators.note: ruined material has been spoilt and jumbled, so these letters are rearranged

explanation.surface: Some fabric's dye has run and spoilt it.
explanation.walkthrough: 'ruined' rearranges RUN and MATERIAL; the 's of 'Colour's' is 'is', linking definition to wordplay.
explanation.definitionFit: Ultramarine is a deep vivid blue pigment, an example of a colour.

clue.text: Found sole in dock

indicators.note: the sole word sits inside the word for dock

parts.note: a pier is a landing stage, a dock
sole means only, one

explanation.surface: A flatfish has been discovered by the harbour.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Found' is a verb meaning establish, not 'discovered', and 'sole' is not the fish.
explanation.definitionFit: To pioneer is to found or originate something new, a verb synonym.

clue.text: Set criminal prisoner back around middle of stretch

parts.note: a con is a convict, a criminal

indicators.note: the turned prisoner goes around the middle of stretch
back means the word for prisoner is read backwards

parts.note: lag is slang for a prisoner, as in old lag

indicators.note: the middle letter of the seven-letter word stretch

explanation.surface: A convict returns an inmate in the middle of his sentence.
explanation.walkthrough: 'back' turns LAG into GAL, then 'around' puts E (the centre of STRETCH) inside it. 'Stretch' is slang for a prison term, part of the surface.
explanation.definitionFit: To congeal is to set or solidify, as jelly or fat does.

clue.text: Right oven for Sunday lunch?

parts.note: an oast is a kiln for drying hops, a kind of oven

explanation.surface: Is this the proper oven to cook the weekend meal?
explanation.walkthrough: An OAST is a kiln for drying hops, familiar in Kent, England.
explanation.definitionFit: A roast dinner is the traditional British Sunday lunch, so this is an example, hence the question mark.

clue.text: Morse perhaps, stern cop I fancy

indicators.note: fancy as an adjective means elaborate or fanciful, so these letters are rearranged

explanation.surface: A severe policeman, rather like Morse, I imagine.
explanation.walkthrough: Inspector Morse is the Oxford detective of the British TV series; 'perhaps' marks him as an example.
explanation.definitionFit: Morse holds the rank of inspector, so he is an example of one.

clue.text: Blab about former PM covering up

indicators.note: the word for blab goes around the former prime minister

parts.note: to sing is slang for informing, blabbing
Edward Heath was a British Prime Minister (1970-74)

explanation.surface: Someone spills the beans about an ex-premier's cover-up.
explanation.definitionFit: Sheathing is the act of covering or encasing something, as a sword in its sheath.

clue.text: Plant elms and tie to switch

indicators.note: to switch is to change round, so these letters are rearranged

explanation.surface: A gardener is told to tie elms to a thin twig.
explanation.walkthrough: 'switch' looks like a thin stick, but it is the anagram signal for ELMS, TIE and TO.
explanation.definitionFit: Mistletoe is a parasitic evergreen plant growing on trees.

clue.text: Struggled with street rent

parts.note: rent as a past participle means torn apart, riven

explanation.surface: A tenant battled with the rent on their street.
explanation.walkthrough: 'rent' looks like a payment, but here it is the past participle of 'rend'.
explanation.definitionFit: Striven is the past participle of strive, to struggle or try hard.

clue.text: Escape the French, returning for example with alias

parts.note: le is French for the
aka, also known as, introduces an alias

indicators.note: returning means the abbreviation for for example is read backwards

explanation.surface: A Frenchman returns under a false name in his escape.
explanation.definitionFit: A leakage is an escape of gas or liquid, a noun synonym.

clue.text: Power for first of trains in line

indicators.note: the first letter of trains is put inside the word for line

parts.note: a seam is a line where two pieces are joined

indicators.note: the first letter of trains

explanation.surface: The energy for the leading locomotives runs in a line.
explanation.definitionFit: Steam is a source of power, as in steam engines.

clue.text: Two days in rocky seat's most painful

indicators.note: the two days sit inside the rearranged seat's
something rocky is unsteady and shaky, so these letters are rearranged

parts.note: the possessive s is kept here as a letter of the fodder
D is the abbreviation for day, so two days is DD

explanation.surface: Sitting on a wobbly chair for two days is agony.
explanation.walkthrough: 'rocky' rearranges the letters of seat's (the S counts here) into SAEST; 'in' then places the two days inside, after SA.
explanation.definitionFit: Saddest means most sorrowful, the most painful to feel.

clue.text: European Commission retreat, sweet for the French!

parts.note: a lair is a hiding place or retreat

explanation.surface: Brussels bureaucrats back off, leaving a treat for France.
explanation.definitionFit: An eclair is a French cream-filled pastry, a sweet of French origin.

clue.text: Read published retraction in front of judge

indicators.note: the turned word goes before the word for judge
a retraction draws back, so the word for published is read backwards

parts.note: ran as in the paper ran the story, published it
to rate is to judge or assess

explanation.surface: A newspaper prints a withdrawal before a judge.
explanation.definitionFit: To read a story aloud is to narrate it, a verb synonym.

clue.text: English leading opening match

indicators.note: English leads, so its letter comes before the word for opening

parts.note: a vent is an opening or outlet

explanation.surface: England is ahead at the start of a game.
explanation.definitionFit: An event is a contest or match in a sporting programme.

clue.text: Tot, more rum left, swallowed after time

indicators.note: the rest of the wordplay comes after the time letter
the word for left is swallowed inside the word for more rum

parts.note: rum means odd, so more rum is odder

explanation.surface: A tot of rum is taken, and more rum knocked back after a while.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Tot' and 'rum' suggest a measure of spirit; 'rum' is British slang for strange.
explanation.definitionFit: A tot is a small child, and a toddler is a young child learning to walk.

clue.text: Had a bite outside by fly

indicators.note: the eating word goes outside the word for by

parts.note: ate means had something to eat
via means by way of

explanation.surface: An insect bit someone outside, beside the fly.
explanation.definitionFit: To aviate is to pilot an aircraft, to fly.

clue.text: Transcriber I anticipate penning 'Man of la Mancha'?

indicators.note: penning means enclosing, so the answer is held inside these words

explanation.surface: A copyist expects to write out the musical about Don Quixote.
explanation.walkthrough: Man of La Mancha is the musical about Don Quixote; La Mancha is in Spain, so a man from there is an Iberian, hence the question mark.
explanation.definitionFit: A man from La Mancha in Spain is a native of the Iberian peninsula.

clue.text: Spy, shirtless perhaps, that is holding gun

parts.note: someone without a shirt may be wearing just a vest, in a vest

indicators.note: the that-is abbreviation holds the gun inside it

parts.note: gat is slang for a gun

explanation.surface: A secret agent, perhaps stripped to the waist, is carrying a weapon.
explanation.walkthrough: In British English a vest is a sleeveless undershirt; a man in a vest without a shirt is 'in vest'.
explanation.definitionFit: To spy into something is to investigate it, examine it closely.
